labels.og_answer: The largest Stegosaurus were about 9 m (30 ft) long, and Sophie in London is about 5.6 m

top.answer: The largest Stegosaurus were about 9 m (30 ft) long, a round figure of London's Natural History Museum, with no skeleton named. Sophie, the famous skeleton in that museum, is about 5.6 m (18 ft) long, from a young animal that was still growing. A 3D model of the skeleton gives about 1.6 tonnes (1.1 to 2.3), and no height of a living Stegosaurus has been published. Ours, built after Sophie, is 5.6 m (18 ft) long, its back 1.9 m (6.4 ft) high over the hips, above a person's head.
top.answer_more: Along its back stood two rows of tall bony plates, left and right in turn, never in pairs. Its tail ended in four spikes that pointed out to the sides, not up.

guess.q: How did Sophie's skeleton first come to light?
guess.a: By accident, in 2003. A man moving a bulldozer on a Wyoming ranch late one evening in a windstorm grazed a hillside, and the next morning bones showed in the slope.

paras: Sophie has 18 plates, and a gap over the tail's base suggests a 19th stood there. The London mount shows 19, one a cast. They stood upright in two rows, left and right in turn, set in the skin, not joined to the skeleton.

The largest is 78.5 cm (2.6 ft) at its longest, in bone, part of it plaster. A smooth layer of horn most likely covered the plates, but its only print comes from one plate of a close relative, Hesperosaurus.

What they were for, nobody knows for sure. Most recent studies favour showing off, a sign by which Stegosaurus could recognise their own kind. Shedding heat, an idea of 1976, was at most a side use. Defence is the weakest idea: the plates were thin, and a tissue study found nothing that would let them move.

Sophie's four tail spikes, in two pairs, are 35 to 38 cm (14 to 15 in) of bone, their tips missing, and horn sheaths made them a little longer. They pointed out to the sides and back, close to level, as another skeleton with its tail bones in place suggests, though Sophie's mount holds them raised.
Many sites give 60 to 90 cm (2 to 3 ft) a spike. That figure comes from a study of 1998 on another skeleton, from Colorado, and Sophie was a young animal.

Most likely they were weapons. Of 51 stegosaur spikes from North America's Morrison Formation, about one in ten has a broken tip, some healed. One Allosaurus tail bone even has a hole that a spike tip fits. The nickname thagomizer began as a joke in a Far Side cartoon of the early 1980s, and scientists took it up informally.

For so big a body, Stegosaurus had a very small brain. The space for it in the skull has long been likened to a walnut, by the London museum to a plum, but a reptile's brain does not fill it, so the brain was smaller still.
Many sites give a figure in grams for its brain. Such figures rest on a cast of the brain space, which the brain did not fill, so they can only be an upper limit.

In the 1880s and 1890s Othniel Marsh found a space in the backbone over the hips at least twenty times as big as the brain's, and called it, carefully, a rear brain case. There was no “second brain”. As in birds, the space most likely held a soft lump of tissue rich in glycogen, a stored sugar. What it did is not settled.

blocks.nav: Sophie, the Stegosaurus skeleton in London
blocks.h: Sophie, the Stegosaurus skeleton in London
paras: Sophie, a Stegosaurus stenops, was found in 2003 on a ranch near Shell, Wyoming, dug up in 2004 and prepared at the Sauriermuseum Aathal in Switzerland. London's Natural History Museum, whose scientists had seen a cast of it at a fair in Tucson in 2012, bought the skeleton with donors' help and has shown it since December 2014. The name honours a donor's daughter: whether Sophie was male or female, nobody knows.

With about 360 bones, Sophie is one of the most complete skeletons of Stegosaurus known. Missing are the left arm, both hands, most of the tail's base and some smaller bones, as well as skin and throat armour. The skull on show is a cast. How Sophie died, nobody knows: the bones show no bite or wound, and the scientists who described them consider starvation or an illness the likeliest causes.
The skeleton picture shows which of our bones are Sophie's own.

scale.what: Our Stegosaurus as a skeleton, at the side view's scale, with Sophie's own bones and the rebuilt ones in two tones.
scale.alt: Our Stegosaurus as a skeleton from the side, beside the grey person: most bones in the tone of Sophie's own, and in the rebuilt tone the front feet, most toes, a shoulder bone, several neck ribs, one plate, the first part of the tail and most of the small bones under it.
key: Rebuilt bones are mirrored from Sophie's other side or modelled on Sophie's neighbouring bones and on other finds. Sophie's bones are shown uncrushed, and some rib ends and plate edges marked as Sophie's are plaster on the real skeleton. The first three tail bones show as rebuilt, though the upper parts of the first three were found. The skull's rebuilt patches are approximate.

blocks.nav: What a real Stegosaurus looked like
blocks.h: What a real Stegosaurus looked like

paras: It had a small, low head, a horny beak and small leaf-shaped teeth. One study of Sophie's skull found a bite like a cow's or a sheep's.
The front legs were shorter than the hind legs, and it walked on all four. Each front foot was a stump of upright palm bones with two small hooves.
Skin is known only from a close relative, Hesperosaurus: small six-sided scales. Other Stegosaurus had small bony bits in the throat skin. No stegosaur's colour is known, so ours is a choice.

blocks.nav: Stegosaurus vs T. rex and Triceratops
blocks.h: Stegosaurus vs T. rex and Triceratops
paras: Stegosaurus never met T. rex or Triceratops. About 80 million years lay between the last Stegosaurus and the first T. rex or Triceratops, at least about 75. That is more than the 66 million years between the last T. rex and us, so T. rex is nearer to us in time than to Stegosaurus. Films that show them meeting are fiction. Stegosaurus's own neighbours included the long-necked Diplodocus and the meat-eater Allosaurus.
In the picture, our T. rex is twice as long as our Stegosaurus, whose tallest plate tip stands about as high as our Triceratops's back.

scale.what: Our Stegosaurus, Triceratops and T. rex to one scale, facing the same way, for size only. About 80 million years lay between Stegosaurus and the other two: the three never met.
scale.alt: Three dinosaurs in three rows, all from the side and facing the same way, each beside the grey person: a Stegosaurus with plates and tail spikes, a Triceratops with horns and a frill, and a T. rex on two legs, twice as long as the Stegosaurus.

paras: Stegosaurus lived in western North America late in the Jurassic, and one skeleton comes from Portugal. The American finds lie in the Morrison Formation, whose dated layers are about 157 to 150 million years old, the top a little younger. Sophie lived about 150 million years ago, by the London museum's figure. Its fossils end before the Cretaceous, which began about 143 million years ago, and nobody knows why.

rows.text: The largest Stegosaurus, not a typical one. Apex in New York is reported as the biggest skeleton on show, at about 8.2 m (27 ft).
Sophie's mount at its highest point, with the tail raised, not a height the animal stood at. None has been published.

No study we read gives either. None gives a height or a weight for a named full-grown Stegosaurus. Popular dinosaur books give the largest up to about 5 tonnes, a book estimate for full-grown animals, not a model of a skeleton.

Both come from leg-bone methods, which ran high for Sophie: up to 3.75 tonnes, a figure the same study rejected. The over 7 tonnes is one very large stegosaur, genus not given, from a meeting abstract of 2025 whose authors say it holds only if their methods are right.
Marsh's rear brain case in the hips, of the 1880s and 1890s. A study of 1990 found no sign of a brain there in living or fossil reptiles.

rows.term: Plates in pairs, and eight spikes
rows.text: Both come from old reconstructions of the 1890s. Skeletons with their plates in place, Sophie among them, show them alternating, and one reconstruction's eight spikes came from two animals.

blocks.intro: For each picture: where it came from, and what we know now.

rows.term: Plates lying flat, like a turtle's shell
rows.text: The very first idea, and the reason for the name roof lizard. We know the plates stood upright: skeletons found with their plates still in place show it.

rows.term: One row of plates down the middle of the back
rows.text: That comes from a drawing of the skeleton made in 1891. Sophie's plates were found mostly where they had lain, in two rows, and other skeletons agree, so we know there were two.

rows.term: A tail dragging on the ground
rows.text: For decades in the 1900s, Stegosaurus was drawn and mounted that way. Going by its bones, the tail was most likely held off the ground, stiff in a few long sections.

rows.term: A hunched back and a tiny neck
rows.text: Many older skeletons on show were put together from several animals. Sophie, one animal and nearly complete, has a longer neck, a shorter body and a less hunched back, which is most likely the better guide.

rows.term: Rearing up on the hind legs, the tail as a third leg
rows.text: An idea since the 1890s. Some scientists doubt it, others find it possible, and nobody knows yet.

items.a: By a 3D model of the skeleton, Sophie, a young animal, comes to about 1.6 tonnes (1.1 to 2.3), a small rhino's weight, says the London museum. Leg-bone rules give more, since a young animal's legs are thick for its weight. For the biggest Stegosaurus, no study we read gives a weight. Popular dinosaur books give a grown Stegosaurus stenops about 6.5 m (21 ft) and 3.5 tonnes, and the largest up to about 5 tonnes. Those are book estimates for full-grown animals, while Sophie's 1.6 tonnes comes from a model of a young one.

items.q: What does the name Stegosaurus mean?
items.a: Roof lizard, from Greek, after Othniel Marsh's first idea in 1877 that the scattered plates had lain flat over the back like roof tiles.

paras: Museum of Ages is a digital museum, made by a nonprofit. Free entry, no account. In the animal wing this animal will stand among the others, from the giants of long ago to the last of their kind. The Leonardo da Vinci wing shows what a finished wing looks like.

items.alt: Our seven dinosaurs in a row from the side, to one scale. The longest, our Argentinosaurus, is about 30.6 m (100 ft) long. Two long necks tower over the rest, and a grey person 1.70 m tall looks tiny beside them.
items.line: Seven of ours beside a person, to one scale: the heaviest most likely a titanosaur from Patagonia, the tallest probably Sauroposeidon, and why the longest is still open.

items.alt: Our Triceratops from the side, 6.9 m (23 ft) from beak to tail and 2.5 m (8 ft) high over the hips: a wide frill behind the head, two long horns over the eyes, a short one on the nose, four legs. Beside it a grey person 1.70 m tall who reaches about two thirds of the way up its back.
items.line: A big adult Triceratops was about 7 to 8 m long, and two models give about 6.5 to 8.5 tonnes for the Washington skeleton, a mount of about ten animals. Our Triceratops stands beside a person to one scale, with its skull against the person, Torosaurus and what the bones say about T. rex.

items.alt: Our T. rex from the side on two legs, about 11 m (36 ft) long in this pose, mouth closed and head raised, beside a grey person 1.70 m tall who stands far below its hips.
items.line: A large adult T. rex was about 12 m long, about 4 m at the hips and roughly 8 to 9 tonnes. Our T. rex is built to SUE's measurements and stands beside a person to one scale, with a list of what was found of SUE.

items.alt: Our Ankylosaurus from the side, 6.4 m (21 ft) from beak to club, its back 1.7 m (5.6 ft) high over the hips: a low, wide body under rows of bony plates, a broad head carried low, four short legs and a straight tail ending in a flat club. Beside it a grey person 1.70 m tall, as tall as the top of its back.
items.line: Ankylosaurus was about 6 to 8 m long, by a 2017 study. The animal with the only tail club found came to about 4.8 tonnes, worked out from its leg bones. Our Ankylosaurus is built at that animal's size and stands beside a person to one scale, with its club, its armour, what was found and what the bones say about T. rex.
